title: The hook nobody can bypass: pre-receive on the server
summary: Client hooks are advisory. Install a pre-receive hook in the bare repository that rejects direct pushes to main and force pushes — and watch --no-verify fail to help.
mental_model: `pre-receive` runs once per push on the server and reads lines of `<old-sha> <new-sha> <ref>` on stdin. Exit non-zero and the entire push is rejected atomically — nothing lands.

steps.title: Confirm the client-side gap
steps.why: Whatever you install locally, anyone can pass `--no-verify`, or push from a machine that never installed your hooks. The server is the only place a rule is actually a rule.

steps.title: Install a pre-receive hook on the server
steps.why: It reads ref updates from stdin. A new sha of all zeroes means a branch deletion; an old sha of all zeroes means creation. Comparing with `merge-base --is-ancestor` detects a force push.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Server-side branch protection for main.

ZERO=0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
status=0

while read old new ref; do
  case "$ref" in
    refs/heads/main)
      if [ "$new" = "$ZERO" ]; then
        echo "pre-receive: refusing to delete main" >&2
        status=1
        continue
      fi

      if [ "$old" != "$ZERO" ] && ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "$old" "$new"; then
        echo "pre-receive: refusing force push to main (would discard commits)" >&2
        status=1
        continue
      fi

      # Every commit reaching main must be a merge, or carry a Refs: trailer.
      for sha in $(git rev-list "$old".."$new" 2>/dev/null || git rev-list "$new"); do
        parents=$(git rev-list --parents -n 1 "$sha" | wc -w)
        if [ "$parents" -ge 3 ]; then
          continue
        fi
        if ! git log -1 --format=%B "$sha" | grep -q '^Refs: '; then
          subject=$(git log -1 --format=%s "$sha")
          echo "pre-receive: $sha ('$subject') has no 'Refs:' trailer" >&2
          status=1
        fi
      done
      ;;
  esac
done

if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "pre-receive: push rejected. Open a pull request instead." >&2
fi

exit $status

verify.label: the server hook is installed and executable

steps.title: Push a commit with no ticket reference
steps.why: The hook walks every commit in the push and checks its message. One failure rejects the whole push — no partial application, which is what makes server hooks trustworthy.
steps.expect: remote: pre-receive: ... has no 'Refs:' trailer, and the push is rejected.

verify.label: the server still has only the original commit

steps.title: Try to bypass it
steps.why: `--no-verify` skips *client* hooks. The server never sees that flag and does not care. This is the whole point: policy enforced where the code lands, not where it is written.

verify.label: --no-verify did not help — server hooks cannot be bypassed

steps.title: Comply with the rule
steps.why: Amend the message to include the trailer the policy requires. Now the push is accepted — the rule was never about obstruction, it was about making history traceable.

actions.run: git commit -q --amend -m "Raise the pump speed" --trailer "Refs: ABH-204"

verify.label: the compliant push was accepted
verify.hint: add a Refs: trailer to the commit message

steps.title: Try a force push that would discard history
steps.why: Resetting back and force-pushing would delete a commit from the server. `merge-base --is-ancestor` catches exactly that case, while allowing ordinary fast-forwards.
steps.expect: pre-receive: refusing force push to main.

verify.label: the force push was refused and the commit survived
verify.hint: the hook compares old and new with merge-base --is-ancestor

steps.title: And a branch deletion
steps.why: A push with an all-zeroes new sha is a deletion. Blocking it for main is the last piece of branch protection — the same three rules GitHub's protected branches implement, in thirty lines of shell.

verify.label: main still exists on the server
the compliant commit reached the server
verify.hint: add a Refs: trailer, then push

verify.label: the server hook is in place

pitfalls: `pre-receive` runs once for the whole push; `update` runs once per ref. Use `update` when you want per-branch rules with independent outcomes.
Write diagnostics to stderr — git prefixes them with 'remote:' and shows them to the pusher. Anything on stdout is far less visible.
The hook runs on the server with the bare repository as its working directory. There is no working tree, so `git checkout` and friends will not behave as you expect.
Hosted forges do not let you install pre-receive hooks on ordinary plans. Their branch-protection settings are the same idea, managed for you.
A slow server hook slows every push for everyone. Keep the checks cheap and push heavy validation into CI.
